one_liner: Templated C++20/23 array/tensor library with SIMD, OpenMP, CUDA and OpenCL backends; beats naive std::vector loops on elementwise math.
what_it_does: LibRapid provides a templated multidimensional Array/tensor class with lazy expression-template evaluation, replacing hand-written nested std::vector loops for elementwise and linear-algebra math. Arrays are built via lrc::Array<T> with an explicit Shape, indexed with operator[], and combined with ordinary arithmetic operators that the library fuses into a single vectorized pass at compile time. It also bundles complex numbers, multiprecision arithmetic (custom MPIR/MPFR forks), FFT (pocketfft/FFTW), BLAS-backed linear algebra and neural-network activation functions, plus optional Python bindings. It is not a drop-in for std::vector/std::valarray; call sites must be rewritten against LibRapid's own container and expression API.
how_it_is_fast: Elementwise expressions like aa * bb - cc are built as an expression tree and evaluated in one fused pass instead of allocating a temporary per operator, then dispatched to SIMD kernels (via the bundled Vc library) and OpenMP threads, or offloaded to CUDA/OpenCL/BLAS backends chosen with a template parameter. Linear-algebra expressions get compile-time rewriting into a single BLAS-style call, e.g. dot(3*a, 2*transpose(b)) becomes one GEMM with alpha/beta/transpose flags folded in. The one verified benchmark compares this fused, vectorized path against naive triple-nested std::vector<std::vector<double>> loops, which allocate a temporary per operator and get no fusion.
when_to_use: Elementwise or linear-algebra-heavy numeric code currently written as nested std::vector loops, on x86-64 with AVX/SSE
Willing to standardize on one array/tensor type across CPU, CUDA and OpenCL backends via a template parameter instead of separate GPU code paths
C++20/23 toolchain available and OK pulling in a CMake build with several optional native dependencies (fmt, Vc, CLBlast, pocketfft, OpenBLAS, MPIR/MPFR, FFTW)
Want BLAS-backed GEMM, FFT, complex/multiprecision arithmetic and NN activation functions from one library instead of assembling Eigen + FFTW + Boost.Multiprecision
Prototyping or research code where a small, actively-evolving (though currently stalled) single-maintainer library is an acceptable risk
when_not_to_use: Need a drop-in replacement for std::vector/std::valarray: requires rewriting to lrc::Array<T> and its own Shape/indexing API, not a header swap
Need OpenCL on Apple Silicon: issue #245 (open since 2023) tracks OpenCL support on macOS Mx as unresolved
Rely on array slicing or generic array views: slicing (#139) and OpenCL GeneralArrayView (#253) are both open and labeled 'Requires Rewrite' since 2023

Need automatic differentiation or trig functions to be bug-free: open issues from Aug 2025 report bugs in the AD product-rule implementation (#273) and in trig functions (#270), filed the week before the project's last commit
Need active maintenance: solo student-maintainer project, last commit 2025-08-21, 15 open issues including 4 unresolved bugs filed just before that final commit

integration.form: source-drop, CMake build (not header-only — CMakeLists globs .hpp under librapid/include plus .cpp/.cxx under librapid/src and cxxblas into a compiled target)
integration.dependencies: bundled submodules: fmt, Vc (SIMD), pocketfft, scnlib, CLBlast, Jitify; optional external: OpenMP, CUDA, OpenCL, OpenBLAS, MPIR, MPFR, FFTW, toggled via CMake options
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 minimum (CMake enforces this with a FATAL_ERROR check), C++23 used by default when built standalone; CMake >= 3.16
integration.platforms: x86-64 primary target (bundles Vc SIMD, LIBRAPID_NATIVE_ARCH on by default); Linux/macOS/Windows for CPU backend; CUDA and OpenCL backends optional and platform-gated, with OpenCL on Apple Silicon macOS unresolved (issue #245)
integration.thread_safety: not documented — OpenMP is used internally to parallelize array operations, but no stated guarantee for concurrent access to the same Array from multiple threads
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false — replaces std::vector-based code with LibRapid's own Array<T>/Shape/expression-template API; call sites must be rewritten, it is not a header swap

gotchas: 'Optimise Small Arrays' is a separate opt-in CMake option (LIBRAPID_OPTIMISE_SMALL_ARRAYS, OFF by default and OFF in the published benchmark), so small-array performance without it is untested by the cited numbers

The benchmark's std::vector baseline is naive nested loops, not std::valarray or a vectorization-friendly std::transform/std::reduce pipeline, so the measured ratio likely overstates the gap versus a tuned STL baseline
Array slicing and generic array views are flagged 'Requires Rewrite' in open issues (#139, #253) rather than treated as stable
The top-level CMakeLists forces BUILD_SHARED_LIBS off on Windows, so shared-library builds aren't exercised on that platform
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick LibRapid over the sibling scalar-math libraries (SLEEF, VDT, fmath, trigno_simd_cpp, FABE13-HX, fast_math_cpp) when the need is a whole array/tensor container with fused elementwise expressions and optional GPU backends, not a faster std::sin/exp/log drop-in; pick Axiom instead if the goal is specifically an Eigen-compatible elementwise-math replacement, since Axiom benchmarks against Eigen3's array ops rather than raw std::vector loops.
verified_claims_summary: First-party dev.to benchmark: elementwise res = aa*bb-cc on 1000x1000 double arrays, run repeatedly (~15,000 iterations), averaged 1.589ms/iteration for naive nested std::vector<std::vector<double>> loops vs 284.405us/iteration for LibRapid's Array, a ~5.59x ratio (the page's '558.71%' is that ratio expressed as a percentage, not '558.71% faster'). Measured on MSVC 19.33 with default project settings, AMD Ryzen 9 3950X, Windows 10 Pro, with LibRapid's 'Optimise Small Arrays' option off.
status_note: Stale: solo student-maintainer project, last commit 2025-08-21, with 4 unresolved bug reports (autodiff product rule, indexing, trig functions, CUDA typo) filed the week before that last commit; MIT-licensed, but its CMake build with multiple optional native/GPU dependencies makes it a heavier vendor than a header-only library.
